items.prompt: Which best describes persuasive design?
choices: Any design that tries to change what the user does next
Influence that works by giving users true, relevant facts
Influence that works by hiding the choice the business dislikes
items.explanation: Persuasion informs the decision. Hiding options is the opposite, and almost all design tries to change behaviour, so that alone cannot be the test.

items.prompt: What is the dividing line between persuasion and manipulation?
choices: Whether the business earns money from the final result
Whether it informs the choice or degrades the ability to make it
Whether the design tries to influence the user's next action at all
items.explanation: Nearly every design influences and nearly every business earns money. The line is about the mechanism.

items.prompt: A row of recommendations built from items the user already viewed is usually...
choices: A dark pattern
Illegal in every case
Ordinary persuasion
items.explanation: It offers relevant, true help with a choice and the user stays free to ignore it.

items.prompt: Informed consent means a user's yes was given...
choices: After scrolling past a long legal document to the end
With accurate facts, freely, and without engineered friction
After a single click on a large bright green button
items.explanation: Consent counts only when the user could see the facts and was not pushed down one path. Big buttons and unread documents show neither.

items.prompt: Which statement would fail the 'say it out loud' check?
choices: We highlight our best-sellers
We hid the cancel link on purpose
We show the price before checkout
items.explanation: Saying the hiding out loud sounds like an admission. The other two can be said to users without damaging trust.

items.prompt: A fake 'Only 2 left!' counter works by...
choices: Giving the shopper better product details
Reducing the number of steps to buy
Exploiting urgency with false information
items.explanation: The counter is false, so it manipulates rather than informs, and urgency pushes people to decide before thinking.

items.prompt: When a dark pattern works, who mostly benefits?
choices: The business, at the user's expense
Both sides roughly equally
The user, at the business's expense
items.explanation: That imbalance is one of the table rows that separate persuasion from manipulation.

items.prompt: Can a design mislead without stating anything false?
choices: No, only outright lies can ever mislead
No, layout never affects what people choose
Yes, by burying or hiding true facts
items.explanation: Placement, timing and size decide whether a true fact is actually seen, so burying it can degrade choice.

items.prompt: A shop shows 'Bestseller' on items that really sold most last month, and a different shop shows 'Bestseller' on whatever it wants to clear. Which is persuasion?
choices: The second, since clearing stock helps the shopper too
Neither, since both labels try to change shopper behaviour
Both, since a label is never a false statement
The first, since its label is true and aids comparison
items.explanation: The test is whether the information is true and relevant. A label on real best-sellers informs; the same label used as an arbitrary lever does not.
items.reference:
Persuade or manipulate?
✅ true, relevant facts that help the decision
✅ survives being said out loud to the user
🚫 false, hidden or irrelevant facts
🚫 works by exploiting urgency, shame or fatigue
Why: nearly all design influences; the line is whether the influence informs the choice or degrades it.
items.learnMore:
The line is how, not whether

Almost every interface tries to change what you do next. What matters is the mechanism: better information for the user, or a weaker ability to choose freely.

Common mistake

Treating any attempt at influence as manipulation, or treating anything technically true as fine.
items.reflection: Think of a shop, a school or a club you know. Where does it nudge you honestly, and where does it quietly make one choice harder than the other?

items.prompt: A page states the monthly price truthfully, but in grey text under a large 'Free for 7 days' headline. Why can this still be manipulative?
choices: Any price shown beneath a bold headline counts as a lie by omission
Free trials always hide their real price
Grey text is banned from commercial pages
The fact is true but placed so the user is unlikely to weigh it
items.explanation: Truth is necessary but not sufficient. Size and placement decide whether the information can inform the decision at all.

items.prompt: A team debates two ways to raise sign-ups by 10 percent: add real customer ratings, or pre-tick a box that shares the user's data. Which discriminates correctly?
choices: Only the ratings are manipulation, since ratings can be gamed by sellers

Both are manipulation because both nudge the user toward signing up
Both are persuasion because both raised sign-ups
items.explanation: Same metric movement, different mechanism. The pre-ticked box works only if the user misses it, which fails the disclosure check.

items.prompt: Which situation best shows informed consent being undermined, even though the user clicked 'Accept'?
choices: The accept button was blue and sat at the top of the dialog
The dialog appeared on the first visit to the website
The decline option was a faint link beneath a wall of text
The user read the full page and then chose to accept
items.explanation: Consent is judged by the conditions under which the click happened. A buried decline makes the yes a product of the layout.

items.prompt: A roach motel makes leaving...
choices: Easier than joining
Exactly as easy as joining
Harder than joining
items.explanation: Easy in, hard out is the whole shape. Equal effort both ways is fair design.

items.prompt: Confirmshaming is when the decline option is...
choices: Worded to make the user feel guilty
Repeated until the user finally accepts
Hidden behind three menus and a link
items.explanation: The label itself carries the guilt, such as 'No thanks, I don't like saving money'.

items.prompt: Forced continuity usually means...
choices: A discount code that expires on a fixed calendar date
A subscription that renews only after the user opts in
A free trial that becomes paid without a clear reminder
items.explanation: The pattern depends on the user forgetting a charge that was always going to happen.

items.prompt: Hidden costs are when...
choices: The real total first appears at the final checkout step
The price is stated clearly on the very first page
Tax is listed as a separate line before payment
items.explanation: A cost revealed only after the user has invested effort exploits the wish not to start over.

items.prompt: A checkbox reading 'Don't not send me updates' is an example of...
choices: A forced continuity
A trick question
A hidden cost
items.explanation: The double negative flips the answer the user expects to give.

items.prompt: A pop-up asking to enable notifications on every single visit is...
choices: Forced continuity
A hidden cost
Nagging
items.explanation: Repeating the request until the user gives in is the defining move.

items.prompt: Why learn the families rather than a list of examples?
choices: Examples never recur in any other product
Each family keeps reappearing in new products
Every family is already banned in every single country
items.explanation: A family names the weakness being exploited, so it transfers to flows nobody has catalogued.

items.prompt: A button labelled 'No thanks, I prefer paying full price' is...
choices: Forced continuity
Confirmshaming
A hidden cost
items.explanation: The wording of the decline carries the guilt, which is the signature of confirmshaming.

items.prompt: A listing shows 'from 9' and the checkout page adds a 4 'service fee' as the final step. Which family fits best?
choices: Forced continuity, since an extra charge was added later in the flow
Nagging, since the fee is shown repeatedly to the buyer
Roach motel, since checkout is hard to leave once begun
Hidden costs, since the real total appears only at the last step
items.explanation: Forced continuity needs a recurring charge the user forgets. A fee revealed at the last step is the hidden-cost shape.
items.reference:
Six recurring shapes
🚪 roach motel: easy in, hard out
😔 confirmshaming: guilt-trip wording on the no
🔁 forced continuity: silent trial-to-paid renewal
🧾 hidden costs: real price shown last
🌀 trick questions: wording flips the answer
🔔 nagging: repeat the ask until they give in
Why: knowing the family lets you spot a brand-new instance of it in a product you have never seen.
items.learnMore:
Recognize the family, not the example

Each family exploits one specific weakness: effort, guilt, forgetfulness, anchoring on a low price, confusing wording or fatigue. New products keep inventing new surfaces for the same six moves.

Common mistake

Memorizing a list of famous examples instead of asking which weakness the flow is leaning on.
items.reflection: Pick one app you use daily. Which of the six families could it drift into if a growth target got tighter, and what would you watch for first?

items.prompt: A service signs you up with one click, but closing the account requires a phone call during office hours. Which family fits best?
choices: Roach motel, because entry and exit effort are deliberately unequal
Confirmshaming, because a phone call feels like a rebuke to leavers
Forced continuity, because the account stays open
Trick question, because the call script may confuse
items.explanation: The defining feature is asymmetry between joining and leaving. No guilt wording or silent renewal is described.

items.prompt: A free trial renews at full price with no reminder, and cancelling takes four screens. Which pair of families is present?

Nagging and forced continuity
Hidden costs and nagging
Confirmshaming and trick questions
items.explanation: The silent conversion is forced continuity; the long exit is the roach motel. They often travel together and reinforce each other.

items.prompt: A form reads 'Uncheck this box if you prefer not to opt out of offers.' Which family is it, and why is it not confirmshaming?
choices: Hidden cost; the box conceals what the user will pay
Trick question; the confusion comes from grammar, not from guilt
Confirmshaming; any confusing label counts as shaming the user
Nagging; the sentence repeats an ask over and over
items.explanation: Trick questions flip the expected answer through wording. Confirmshaming needs an emotional jab at the decline option.

items.prompt: Which is one of the three questions?
choices: Does the page load within two seconds on mobile?
Is the brand colour palette accessible to all users?
Is the effort roughly symmetric between the choices?
items.explanation: Symmetry of effort is question two. Speed and colour are real concerns but not part of this test.

items.prompt: Question one asks whether the needed information is...
choices: Sent in an email on the first day
Written somewhere inside the terms
Visible at the moment the user needs it
items.explanation: Existing somewhere is not enough; it has to be seen in time to matter.

items.prompt: Question three asks whether the team would be comfortable...
choices: Saying the mechanism out loud to the people targeted
Reporting the metric to leadership each quarter
Publishing the full source code to the public
items.explanation: If describing the mechanism sounds like an admission, that is the signal.

items.prompt: A confirmation before deleting years of data is usually...
choices: A legitimate step guarding against a mistake
Proof that the product is a roach motel
Always a dark pattern in every case
items.explanation: It adds a proportionate step to guard against an irreversible error, which serves the user.

items.prompt: How many failed questions point to a dark pattern?
choices: None
Two or three
Exactly one or none
items.explanation: One failure is a signal worth investigating. Two or three together mark a design that has crossed the line.

items.prompt: A single 'no' on one question is...
choices: Irrelevant to the whole review
An automatic dark pattern verdict
A signal, not a verdict
items.explanation: Some friction is legitimate, so one 'no' calls for a closer look.

items.prompt: A reminder email sent 40 minutes before a charge with a vague subject mostly fails...
choices: Question three on its own
Question two: symmetric effort
Question one: visibility
items.explanation: The notice exists but is timed and worded so it is unlikely to be seen and acted on.

items.prompt: One click to sign up but four screens to cancel mostly fails...
choices: None of the three questions
Question one: visible information
Question two: symmetric effort
items.explanation: Effort is unequal between the business-friendly and user-friendly choices.

items.prompt: A trial converts to paid after a single reminder sent 40 minutes before the charge. The team says a reminder 'did go out'. What is the strongest reply?
choices: Any reminder at all passes question one, however it is timed
Reminders only matter for yearly plans, never for monthly ones
Question one asks about being seen in time, not about existing
The reply depends on question three alone, not on timing
items.explanation: Question one is about whether the information can be seen and acted on, not whether a record of it exists.
items.reference:
The three-question test
👁️ 1. is the needed info visible when needed?
⚖️ 2. is the effort roughly symmetric?
🗣️ 3. could the team say the mechanism out loud?
1 'no' = signal; 2 or 3 'no' = dark pattern
Why: each question checks a different way a design can degrade a choice, so fixing one does not clear the others.
items.learnMore:
Three independent checks

Visibility, symmetry and disclosability each catch something the others can miss. A single failed question can be legitimate friction; a cluster of failures all leaning one direction is a strategy.

Common mistake

Fixing the easiest question and declaring the whole flow clean.
items.reflection: Take a flow you have used recently, such as a return, a cancellation or a data-sharing prompt. Run the three questions on it. Which one was hardest to answer honestly?

items.prompt: A cancel flow has three screens, all clearly labelled, each with a true new fact. Sign-up takes one screen. What does the test say?
choices: Question two signals, but one and three pass, so look closer
It is fine because effort never counts in the test at all
It is a dark pattern because three screens exceeds one
It is fine because every screen contains a true statement
items.explanation: One failed question is a signal. The labelling and true content pass the others, so the flow needs a closer look, not an automatic ban.

One plain confirmation before permanently erasing a project
items.explanation: A proportionate confirmation protects the user from an irreversible mistake and passes all three questions.

items.prompt: A retention target rewards...
choices: Only reductions that users chose entirely freely
Any reduction in cancellations, however it happens
Only genuinely better offers made to customers
items.explanation: A metric counts outcomes; it has no idea whether they came from value or from friction.

items.prompt: Most dark patterns usually start from...
choices: Users who misread perfectly clear screens
A designer who is set on deceiving every user
A business metric that ignores how it improved
items.explanation: The common failure is metric pressure, not villainy.

items.prompt: Extra cancel screens showing a real cheaper plan are...
choices: Legitimate persuasion
Always a dark pattern
A hidden cost
items.explanation: They add true, new information to the decision.

items.prompt: Extra screens that repeat 'Are you sure?' with no new facts mainly add...
choices: Effort asymmetry
A better offer
Genuinely new facts
items.explanation: Nothing new is learned, so the only effect is making leaving harder.

items.prompt: A review that only asks 'did the metric move?' will...
choices: Pass anything that moves it
Catch dark patterns very early
Reject every single nudge it sees
items.explanation: Without a how-question, a number improved by friction looks the same as one improved by value.

items.prompt: What tells a better offer from added friction?
choices: The number of screens alone
The size of the dashboard number
The three-question test
items.explanation: The questions look at information, effort and disclosability, which the metric cannot see.

items.prompt: 'A chance to reconsider' framing assumes the extra screens...
choices: Reduce company costs
Inform the user better
Are required by regulation
items.explanation: That assumption has to be checked against what the screens actually say.

items.prompt: Which change to a number is healthy?
choices: Cancellations fell after the link was hidden in settings
Cancellations fell once a cheaper plan was offered
Cancellations fell after a guilt-worded decline button
items.explanation: The first improved because users got something better. The others reduced exits by making them harder.

items.prompt: Retention rose after the team added two cancel screens. What should be checked before celebrating?
choices: Whether the dashboard refreshes in real time for the team
Whether competitors also use the same screens in their flows
Whether the screens add true facts or only add effort
Whether the new screens match the established brand style
items.explanation: The number is ambiguous about cause. The review has to separate value from friction.
items.reference:
A metric cannot tell how it moved
📈 retention up because the offer got better ✅
📈 retention up because leaving got harder 🚫
both look identical on the dashboard
only the three questions tell them apart
Why: a target rewards any improvement of the number, so the review has to ask how the number improved.
items.learnMore:
Why good people ship bad patterns

Most dark patterns are not designed by someone who sets out to deceive. A reasonable target for retention or sign-ups simply rewards whatever moves it, including friction.

Common mistake

Treating a metric improvement as proof that the design is working for users.
items.reflection: Think of a number you are measured on, at work or in study. Name one way it could improve while the people it is meant to serve are worse off.

items.prompt: Two changes each cut cancellations by 10 percent: A offers a prorated refund; B buries the cancel link in a sub-menu. Which statement is correct?

Only B is legitimate because it is cheaper to build
Both moved the metric, but only A passes the three questions
Both fail because any change to cancellation is manipulative
items.explanation: Equal metric movement hides a very different mechanism. Prorated refunds inform and help; burying the link degrades choice.

items.prompt: Sign-up takes 2 steps and cancelling takes 4. The exit-to-entry ratio is...
items.explanation: 4 divided by 2 is 2.0, so leaving takes twice the effort of joining.

items.prompt: With 2 sign-up steps and 6 cancel steps, the ratio is...
items.explanation: 6 divided by 2 is 3.0.

items.prompt: The demo's estimate of abandonment at 1 cancel step is...
items.explanation: The rule is 12 points per step beyond the first, so one step gives zero.

items.prompt: The demo's estimate of abandonment at 4 cancel steps is...
items.explanation: Three extra steps times 12 points gives 36 percent.

items.prompt: The demo's estimate of abandonment at 8 cancel steps is...
items.explanation: Seven extra steps times 12 is 84, below the demo's 85 percent ceiling.

items.prompt: 'Abandoned the cancellation' means the user...
choices: Chose to keep the plan after comparing offers
Cancelled successfully on the last screen
Gave up and stayed without changing their mind
items.explanation: The estimate counts people worn down by the flow, not people who decided to stay.

items.prompt: A ratio of 1.0 means...
choices: Leaving is twice as hard as joining
Joining is impossible for new users
Leaving takes the same effort as joining
items.explanation: Equal effort in and out is the symmetry that question two looks for.

items.prompt: Why compare cancel steps to sign-up steps?
choices: Sign-up is always the longest flow of any product
Step counts do not matter to anyone at all
They show entry and exit effort of one product
items.explanation: A fair benchmark for exit effort is the entry effort of the same product.

items.prompt: Using the demo's assumed rule, how many percentage points does abandonment rise when cancelling grows from 4 to 6 steps?
choices: 36 points
60 points
24 points
12 points
items.explanation: At 4 steps the estimate is 36 percent, at 6 steps it is 60. The difference is 24 points.
items.reference:
Effort in vs. effort out
✍️ sign-up: 2 steps
🚪 cancel: 4 steps → ratio 2.0×
🧭 the demo estimates 36% of users give up at 4 steps
a ratio compares exit to entry of the same product
Why: the ratio shows asymmetry that a raw step count hides.

Automatic within a short window

In the same app where they joined

items.explanation: Self-serve exit matches self-serve entry.

items.prompt: A trial flow now sends a plain reminder on day 13, but cancelling still needs a hidden setting. How should the redesign be judged?
choices: Unfixed, since any hidden setting cancels the reminder out
Fixed, since symmetric effort is optional in a good flow
Fully fixed, since the reminder was the main problem
Partly fixed: visibility returns, but effort stays asymmetric
items.explanation: Each failed question needs its own remedy. The reminder cures question one only.
items.reference:
What a redesigned exit looks like
🚪 one clear cancel control, same clicks as sign-up
🎁 at most one labelled offer, with a real 'no thanks'
📅 renewal date and price shown inside the product
📧 billing-notice reminder 2 to 3 days before the charge
↩️ automatic refund within 24 to 48 hours
Why: each fix restores one of the three questions: visibility, symmetry or disclosability.
items.learnMore:
Keep the offer, remove the engineering

A redesign does not ban retention offers or reminders. It removes the structure that made true statements work against the user: the extra screens, the missable timing and the shamed decline.

Common mistake

Assuming a redesign means deleting all retention efforts.
items.reflection: Choose a flow you would redesign. Which single change would restore the most trust, and what metric would you expect to dip for a while?

In design review before shipping
items.explanation: Fixing it before launch avoids both user harm and enforcement.

Enforcement detects late, so harm happens in the meantime
Legal teams always miss dark patterns in their reviews
Ethics is purely subjective, so no test can apply
items.explanation: Waiting for enforcement treats the regulator as the review process. Harm and reputation costs start at launch.
items.reference:
Regulators read the shape
📐 is leaving harder than joining?
⏱️ is the disclosure timed to be missed?
🌀 is consent obtained through confusion?
no mind-reading: the flow itself is the evidence
Why: these are the same questions as the three-question test, applied by someone with enforcement power.
items.learnMore:
Enforcement is a late detector

Rules and enforcement differ by place and change over time, so check the current position rather than relying on a summary. What stays constant is that regulators describe flows by their shape, which design review can check first.

Common mistake

Reading 'not yet flagged' or 'rule overturned' as 'approved'.
